newsitem.title: INDIA: World Bank targets AIDS in India.
newsitem.headline: World Bank targets AIDS in India.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Monday the fight against AIDS in India was of prime importance to the bank, and he also issued a stern warning that corruption would jeopardise World Bank loans.

"Worldwide...the single most important barrier to effective implementation (of development loan programmes) is corruption," Wolfensohn told a news conference at the end of the first stage of a week-long tour of the country.
"If we find evidence of corruption in our projects we'll just stop them," he said.

Wolfensohn, visiting the bank's biggest borrower for the first time since he took the job last year, has hammered out the warning before and was not singling out India. He said corruption was a problem for developed and developing countries.
But the message will strike a nerve in a country wracked by scandals in high places.
Right at the top, former Prime Minister Narasimha Rao is concurrently facing three separate corruption cases.
But Wolfensohn steered clear of any undiplomatic comment.
"I'm not here to comment on Indian politics or the Indian situation," he said.
He also said he would leave any comment on the progress of India's liberal economic reforms until after he had spoken to central government officials in New Delhi next week.

Wolfensohn visited one of Bombay's infamous red light areas, where according to estimates from the Indian Health Organisation (IHO) around 65 percent of the 70,000 prostitutes working there have been tested positive for the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) -- the virus that leads to AIDS.

He said that he was impressed by the work the government and health workers were doing to halt the spread of the killer disease. The IHO estimates that there are currently four million cases of HIV in India and that figure could reach 15 to 20 million by the end of the century.

"If there is anything that has come home to me on this visit, it is probably that the single most important issue that I have to address when I get back..is the issue of AIDS," Wolfensohn said. "We're committed to that in the Bank. We're the largest single donor to AIDS programmes around the world."
A trip to Bombay's Churchgate railway station for the Monday morning rush hour gave Wolfensohn a taste of how badly the city's urban transport project needs World Bank money.
"Just spending 15 minutes there was enough," he said.

Wolfensohn also visited Bombay slums on Sunday to witness first hand the poverty that 5.5 million of the city's 13 million inhabitants live in -- and saw the need for housing, safe water and sanitation.

He also met with a number of non-government organisation (NGO) representatives who were unhappy at the social and environmental impact of some of the projects that the Bank had funded. He said the Bank was intent on working more with them.

The World Bank funds engaged in active programmes in India are running at $14 billion, seven billion of which has been not yet been spent, and the total lending programme earmarked for India is 28 billion, Wolfensohn said.

Wolfensohn's schedule will take him to the southern city of Bangalore, India's silicon valley, and the eastern state of Orissa where World Bank funds have financed a restructuring of the power sector.
He will meet Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, Finance Minister P.Chidambaram and President Shanker Dayal Sharma in New Delhi on the last leg of his tour ending Ocotber 19.
